Hybrid course after Teach Yourself Dutch and Colloquial Dutch: units 0–8

Hi! My name is Sanne.
I live in a house with a blue door.
I drink coffee with milk.
My bicycle is white and red.
Goodbye!

Dutch uses the ordinary **26 letters** of the Latin alphabet — there are no extra letters like German ä, ö, ü or ß. The letters **q, x, y** and often **c** occur almost only in loanwords. The hard part is not the letters but the **letter combinations** (aa, ee, oe, ui, ij, ch, sch…) — they are explained in the next lessons.

Accents are not separate letters, they only help reading: **ë, ï** (trema) start a new syllable — *België*, *ruïne*; **é, è** mark stress or a vowel in a few words — *één* (one, stressed), *café*, *crème*. **IJ** is written as one unit: at the start of a word both letters are capital — *IJsland*.
How do you spell that? — B-E-L-G-I-Ë.
Spelling your name is a common situation: “Hoe spel je dat?” — How do you spell that?
How many letters are in the Dutch alphabet?
Does Dutch have extra letters like German ä, ö, ü?
What do the two dots in **België** mean?
Say the letter names: aa, bee, cee, dee, ee, ef, gee
Five short vowels, always written with **one letter** in a closed syllable (ending in a consonant): **a** in *man*, **e** in *lek*, **i** in *wit*, **o** in *bot*, **u** in *kus*.
Long vowels: aa, ee, oo, uu
In a closed syllable a long vowel is written **double**: *maan*, *boot*, *leek*, *vuur*. The difference changes the meaning: **man** (man) — **maan** (moon).
All single vowels — how they sound
Approximate sounds (Netherlands pronunciation). In the Netherlands **ee, oo, eu** glide a little at the end: *twee* ≈ “tvey”, *boot* ≈ “bowt”.
Long Dutch vowels are really long: hold them, as in English “baa”. twee is “tvey”, not “tsvey”: w after t is a soft “v”.
Which word has a LONG vowel?
Which word has a SHORT vowel?

An **open** syllable ends in a vowel (*ma-nen*), a **closed** one in a consonant (*man*). In an open syllable a **single** vowel letter is already long: **ma**-nen = “maa-nen”. To keep a vowel short, the consonant is **doubled**: **man-nen**.
Final **-en** is usually pronounced as a weak **-e** (like the *a* in “sofa”): *manen* ≈ “maa-nə”, *boten* ≈ “boo-tə”.
Special vowels: ui, eu, oe, ie, ij/ei, ou/au
German ö: say “e” with rounded lips
German ü: say “ee” with rounded lips
no English sound: “ow” starting from ö
**ij** and **ei** sound the same (*ijs*, *trein*), and so do **ou** and **au** (*zout*, *blauw*). You simply learn the spelling with the word.
In dictionaries ij is often sorted like y, and IJ is capitalised as one letter: IJsland (Iceland).
A book, a house, a door.
Consonants: g, ch, sch, v, w, r
**g** and **ch** are the same throaty sound, like the *ch* in Scottish *loch* or German *Bach* (soft in the south, rough in the north): *gek*, *dag*, *licht*. **sch** = s + ch: *school* ≈ “s-chool”.
s + ch; at the end of words: -isch = “-ies”
softer than English w: almost v
Most consonants sound as in English. The ones to notice:
at the end of a word: p, t
k before a, o, u; s before e, i
without the puff of air of English
l; after a vowel quite dark
s + r (the ch is almost silent)
only in loanwords: i or ee
At the end of a word, **d** and **b** are pronounced **t** and **p**: *goed* ≈ “goet”, *rood* ≈ “root”. -**ig** sounds like “-əch”.
Most Dutch words are stressed on the **first syllable**: *KOF-fie*, *WA-ter*. Exceptions are borrowed words and words with prefixes like *be-*, *ge-*, *ver-*: *be-GRIJ-pen*.
Two dots over a vowel mean a new syllable starts: *Bel-gi-ë*, *ide-ë*. Without them **ie** would be read as one sound.
Hello, come in! Greetings, introductions, drinks

Teacher: Hello, come in! What's your name?
Anna: My name is Anna.
Teacher: Welcome, Anna. Where are you from?
Anna: I'm from Russia.
Teacher: And where do you live?
Anna: I live in Utrecht now.
Teacher: Sit down. This is Tom. He's from England.
Tom: Hi Anna, nice to meet you!

Jos: Hey Maarten! How are you?
Maarten: Fine, and you?
Jos: Great. Sit down. Would you like something to drink?
Maarten: Yes, please. A coffee, please.
Jos: With milk and sugar?
Maarten: With milk, without sugar.
Jos: And I'd like a beer.
**Hallo** and **hoi** are informal, **goedemorgen / goedemiddag / goedenavond** are neutral. **Dag** works for hello *and* goodbye. Goodbye: **tot ziens** (neutral), **doei** (informal).
**Hoe heet je?** — What's your name? (informal). **Hoe heet u?** — formal. Answer: **Ik heet …** or **Ik ben …**. When you meet someone: **Aangenaam!**
What's your name? — My name is Anna.
What's your name (formal)? — My name is De Vries.
Dutch people usually introduce themselves with their first name and shake hands.
You meet someone new. You say:
Good afternoon! My name is Sanne.
Hello, my name is Anna. Pleased to meet you!
Introduce yourself: say hello and your name.
I, you, he… and the verb zijn

Many pronouns have a **stressed** and an **unstressed** form: **jij/je**, **zij/ze**, **wij/we**. In normal speech the short form is more common; the long form adds emphasis. **u** is the polite “you” (to strangers, older people, in shops).
**zijn** is irregular, learn it by heart:
In questions jij comes after the verb: Ben jij student? — Bent u student? (formal).
You talk to an older stranger. “You” is…
You talk to two friends. “You” is…
I'm a student. You are a student too.
Where are you from? Regular verbs

Take the infinitive and drop **-en** to get the **stem**: wonen → **woon** (spelling rule: keep the vowel long, so *woon* with oo). Then: **ik** + stem, **jij/u/hij/zij** + stem **-t**, plural = the infinitive.
When **jij/je** comes *after* the verb (questions), the **-t** disappears: Jij woon**t** in Utrecht. → **Woon** jij in Utrecht? With **u** and **hij** the -t stays: Woont u hier?
Where are you from? — I'm from Russia.
Where do you live? — I live in Utrecht.
Stems never end in a double consonant or v/z: zitten → ik zit, leven → ik leef, lezen → ik lees.
Say where you're from and where you live.

**Hoe gaat het?** — How are you? Formal: **Hoe gaat het met u?** Answers: **goed** (well), **prima** (great), **het gaat** (so-so), **niet zo goed** (not so well). Ask back: **En met jou?** / **En met u?**
How are you? — Great, and you?
How are you (formal)? — Fine, thank you.
**niet** usually goes **after** the verb (and after a pronoun object), but **before** adjectives and place phrases: Ik woon **niet** in Utrecht. Het gaat **niet** goed. Ik ben **niet** Anna.
He doesn't live in the Netherlands.
A friend asks: Hoe gaat het? Answer and ask back.
**Wil je iets drinken?** — Would you like something to drink? (formal: **Wilt u …?**). Accept: **Ja, graag** (yes, please). Refuse: **Nee, dank je / dank u** (no, thanks).
**alsjeblieft** (informal) / **alstublieft** (formal) means both “please” and “here you are”. **dank je / dank u** — thank you. Ordering: **Een koffie, alsjeblieft.**
Would you like a drink? — Yes, please. A tea, please.
With milk and sugar? — Without sugar, thanks.
“Een koffie” or “een kopje koffie” — both are fine. A small beer is “een biertje”.
Would you like something to drink?
Write a short dialogue: offer a friend a drink, they answer and say how they want it (met/zonder).
What do you do? Family, languages, jobs

My name is Lotte and I'm 28. I'm married. My husband is called Daan. He's a cook. I'm a teacher. We have two children: a son and a daughter. My parents live in Groningen. I have a brother, but I don't have a sister.

Lotte: Daan, this is Ivan. He's a friend of my brother's.
Daan: Hi Ivan. Are you Dutch?
Ivan: No, I'm Russian. I'm from Moscow.
Daan: You speak Dutch well!
Ivan: Thanks, I've been learning it for two years.
Daan: What do you do?
Ivan: I'm an engineer. I work at Philips.
Daan: And do you speak German too?
Ivan: A little.
To introduce someone: **Dit is …** (This is …) — for one person or thing, whether man or woman: *Dit is mijn vader. Dit is Lotte.* Plural: **Dit zijn …**
**mijn** = my. **man/vrouw** also mean husband/wife: *mijn man* = my husband.
These are my brother and my sister.
This is my mother and this is my father.
Age is said with **zijn**: **Ik ben 28 (jaar).** Question: **Hoe oud ben je?** / **Hoe oud bent u?**
Numbers 1–12: een, twee, drie, vier, vijf, zes, zeven, acht, negen, tien, elf, twaalf. More numbers come in unit 3.
I have a brother and a sister.
Tell about your family: brothers, sisters, children (hebben).
Nationalities have a male and a female form; the language is usually the neuter adjective, written with a capital letter: *Ik ben Rus/Russische. Ik spreek Russisch.*

**spreken** follows the regular pattern: ik **spreek**, jij **spreekt** (spreek jij?), hij **spreekt**, wij **spreken**. Note the spelling: *spre-ken* (open syllable) → *spreek* (closed, so double ee).
Do you speak Dutch? — Yes, a little.
She's German, but she speaks English well.
He is from Germany. He is…
I'm Russian and I speak Russian and English.
How long has Ivan been learning Dutch?
Say your nationality and which languages you speak.
With **zijn** + job, Dutch uses **no article**: *Ik ben arts.* (I'm a doctor.) *Hij is kok.* Question: **Wat doe je?** / **Wat doet u?** (What do you do?) or **Wat voor werk doe je?**
What do you do? — I'm a nurse.
**doen** has a short stem: ik **doe**, jij **doet** (doe jij?), hij **doet**, wij **doen**. Similarly **gaan**: ik ga, jij gaat, hij gaat, wij gaan.
My father works in an office.
What kind of work do you do?
What do you do? Say your job or what you study and where.
use ik ben / ik werk / ik studeer

Use **geen** instead of *niet een* or before a noun without an article: *Ik heb **een** broer → Ik heb **geen** broer. Ik drink koffie → Ik drink **geen** koffie.* Everything else gets **niet**: *Ik ben **niet** getrouwd. Ik werk **niet**.*
Put the verb first: *Heb je kinderen? — Nee, ik heb geen kinderen.* *Ben je getrouwd? — Nee, ik ben niet getrouwd.*
Rule of thumb: if you could say “een” or nothing before the noun — geen.
I don't have a brother, but I do have a sister.
Do you have children? — No, I don't have children.
Write 4–5 sentences about yourself: name, age, nationality, languages, job, family. Use geen or niet at least once.
Where do you live? Home and neighbourhood

I live in a flat in Utrecht. The flat isn't big, but it is bright. There are two rooms: a living room and a bedroom. The kitchen is small. There's also a balcony. I live with my boyfriend. Our neighbourhood is quiet. There's a supermarket nearby and the station isn't far.

Room for rent in Leiden. Large, bright room on the second floor. Kitchen and bathroom shared with two housemates. Rent: 450 euros a month. The room is close to the station and the university. Call 06-12345678.
Dutch has two words for “the”: **de** (about 2/3 of nouns) and **het**. You have to learn the article with each noun: *de kamer, de tuin, het huis, het balkon*. All plurals take **de**: *de huizen*.

Always **het**: diminutives (*het huisje*), words ending in **-ment** (*het appartement*), most words with **ge-** and **be-** (*het gebouw*). People are almost always **de**: *de man, de vrouw*. **een** (a) is the same for both.
The house is big, but the garden is small.
I have a flat with a balcony.
The house is big and the garden is beautiful.
We have a house with a garden.
How many rooms does the flat have?
I live in a small flat.

Most nouns add **-en**. Watch the spelling rules from unit 0: *de stoel → stoel**en**, het bed → be**dd**en* (short e, double d), *de straat → stra**t**en* (long aa in an open syllable = one a), *het huis → hui**z**en* (s → z), *de brief → brie**v**en* (f → v).

Words ending in unstressed **-el, -em, -en, -er, -je** and many loanwords take **-s**: *de tafel → tafel**s**, de kamer → kamer**s**, de winkel → winkel**s***. Words ending in a vowel take **'s**: *de auto → auto's*.
Irregular: het kind → de kinderen, de stad → de steden.
There are two shops in the street.
a sofa, a table and four chairs
I have two rooms and three cupboards.
Possessives come before the noun. Like pronouns, some have a stressed and an unstressed form (**jouw/je**). Only **ons/onze** changes: **ons** + het-word, **onze** + de-word or plural.
This is our house and this is our garden.
Where's your room? — My room is upstairs.
zijn = “his” and also “to be”: Zijn huis is groot. (His house is big.)
Their house is small, but their garden is big.
Who does the writer live with?
This is our living room and that's my room.
The neighbourhood: er is / er zijn
**Er is** + singular, **er zijn** + plural: *Er **is** een park. Er **zijn** twee supermarkten.* Question: **Is er …? / Zijn er …?** Negative: **Er is geen …**
Is there a supermarket in the area? — Yes, nearby.
There are a lot of shops in our street.
Adjectives after **zijn** have no ending: *De buurt is rustig. Het park is mooi.* Opposites: groot – klein, rustig – druk, dichtbij – ver.
Before a noun adjectives usually get -e: een rustige buurt, een grote kamer — this is in unit 6.
There's a supermarket in the area.
busy: many shops and a big station
quiet: a park and a few houses
Describe your neighbourhood: what is there, is it quiet or busy?
13–19 end in **-tien**: dertien, veertien, vijftien, zestien, zeventien, achttien, negentien. Tens: twintig, dertig, veertig, vijftig, zestig, zeventig, tachtig, negentig, honderd.

Like in German, the units come first, joined with **en** (written as one word): 21 = **eenentwintig** (“one-and-twenty”), 47 = **zevenenveertig**, 85 = **vijfentachtig**. With an umlaut after -e: **tweeënveertig**, **drieënzestig**.
The house number comes **after** the street: *Ik woon in de Kerkstraat, op nummer 12.* Or: *Mijn adres is Kerkstraat 12.* Phone numbers are read in pairs or digit by digit: *06 – 12 34 56 78*.
de verdieping: de begane grond = ground floor, de eerste verdieping = the floor above it (the British “first floor”, the American “second floor”).
What do you share with housemates?
I live on the second floor (two floors above the ground floor).
Write a short ad: your room or flat for rent — size, rooms, floor, rent, neighbourhood (er is / er zijn).
What would you like? (in a shop)

Seller: Good morning, madam. What would you like?
Mrs Bos: May I have a kilo of apples?
Seller: Here you are. Anything else?
Mrs Bos: Yes, a pound of tomatoes and four bananas.
Seller: That's six euros fifty, then.
Mrs Bos: Can I pay by card?
Seller: No, sorry, at the market you have to pay cash.
Mrs Bos: No problem. Here you are, ten euros.
Seller: And three euros fifty change. Thank you!

On Saturday I always do the shopping. I buy bread at the baker's and meat at the butcher's. At the market the vegetables are fresh and cheap. Today I want to buy 100 grams of cheese, a carton of milk, six eggs and a bottle of wine. Wine isn't cheap, but it is tasty!
Food and where to buy it

Many shops are named after the person: **de bakker** (baker's), **de slager** (butcher's), **de groenteboer** (greengrocer). Buy something **bij de bakker** (at the baker's), but **op de markt** (at the market) and **in de supermarkt**.
I buy bread at the baker's.
At the market the vegetables are fresh.
de appel → appels, de banaan → bananen, de aardappel → aardappelen / aardappels, de tomaat → tomaten, het ei → **eieren** (irregular). **groente** and **fruit** are usually used without a plural.
Boodschappen doen = to do the (grocery) shopping. Winkelen = to go shopping for fun (clothes etc.).
I buy meat at the butcher's.
The apples and bananas are fresh.
We do the shopping at the market.
Where does the writer buy bread?
At the market the vegetables are fresh and cheap.

After a quantity word the food follows directly — no word for “of”: **een kilo appels**, **een fles wijn**, **twee pakken melk**. Quantity words stay singular after a number: **twee kilo**, **drie ons**, **vijf liter** (but *twee flessen*, *twee pakken*).
**Hoeveel** = how much / how many: *Hoeveel appels wilt u? — Zes, alstublieft.* *Hoeveel kaas? — Twee ons.*
Shops still say “een pond” (500 g) and “een ons” (100 g) — very common at the market and the cheese counter.
I want two cartons of milk and six eggs.
How much cheese does the writer want?
100 grams of cheese and a carton of milk, please.

**Wat kost …?** / **Hoeveel kost …?** — How much is …? Plural: **Wat kosten de appels?** Answer: *Twee euro.* Prices are said without “and”: **€ 3,50 = drie euro vijftig**. Note: the euro sign comes first, and a **comma** is used for cents.

**pinnen** = pay with a debit card (very common), **contant betalen** = pay cash. *Kan ik pinnen?* — Can I pay by card? *Wilt u de bon?* — Do you want the receipt? *Wilt u een tas?* — Do you want a bag?
“euro” has no plural in prices: tien euro (not euros).
How much is a bottle of wine?
The cheese is tasty but expensive.
How much change does she get?
Ask how much something costs and whether you can pay by card.
Want, can, may, must: modal verbs
Modal verbs + infinitive at the end

A modal verb takes the 2nd place; the main verb goes as an **infinitive to the end** of the sentence: *Ik **wil** vandaag brood **kopen**.* *Je **moet** op de markt contant **betalen**.* Question: ***Kan** ik hier **pinnen**?*
May I have a kilo of apples?
We still have to do the shopping.
“Mag ik …?” without a second verb is the standard polite way to ask for something in a shop.
You can't pay by card here (je after the verb).
I want to buy fish today.
Do I have to pay in cash?
We want to buy a house.
Why can't Mrs Bos pay by card?
at the market you have to pay cash
must still buy bread, but the baker's is closed
Say what you want to buy today and what you still have to do (willen, moeten).
When the seller hands you something, they say **alstublieft** (here you are). You answer **dank u (wel)**. When you pay, you also say **alstublieft**.
The seller asks “What would you like?”:
The seller gives you the bag:
What would you like? (in a shop)
Good morning, may I have six eggs?
May I have a kilo of potatoes?
What does Mrs Bos ask for first?
Why does the writer buy vegetables at the market?
May I have a pound of tomatoes and a kilo of apples?
Write a short dialogue at the market or the cheese shop: greeting, what you want (quantities), price, paying.

I get up at seven every day. First I have a shower and then I have breakfast. I eat bread with cheese and drink coffee. At a quarter past eight I cycle to work. I start at nine. At half past twelve I have lunch with my colleagues. I work until five. After that I do the shopping and go home. I get home at half past six. In the evening I cook, and after dinner I watch TV or read a book. At eleven I go to bed.

Tom: Hi Lisa, it's Tom. Are you free on Saturday?
Lisa: Saturday? I'm working in the morning, but I'm free in the afternoon.
Tom: Great. I'm going to the cinema. Are you coming along?
Lisa: Yes, lovely! What time does the film start?
Tom: At a quarter to eight.
Lisa: Fine. Where shall we meet?
Tom: At half past seven in front of the cinema?
Lisa: OK. Will you phone me when you leave?
Tom: Yes, I will. See you Saturday!
Lisa: See you then!

**Het is drie uur.** — It's three o'clock. Minutes up to 15 go **over** (past), from 45 **voor** (to): *vijf **over** drie* (3:05), *kwart **over** drie* (3:15), *kwart **voor** vier* (3:45), *tien **voor** vier* (3:50).
half = half way TO the next hour

Careful: **half drie** is **2:30**, not 3:30 — literally “half (of the way to) three”. Russian works the same way: «половина третьего». Around the half hour the Dutch count from it: *vijf **voor half** drie* (2:25), *vijf **over half** drie* (2:35).
**Hoe laat is het?** — What time is it? **Hoe laat begint de film?** — What time does the film start? The answer uses **om**: *Om acht uur.* *Om half negen.*
In speech the 12-hour clock is normal; add 's ochtends, 's middags or 's avonds if needed. Timetables use 24 hours: 19.45 uur.
What time does the film start?
Say what time it is now and what time you get up.
Days and parts of the day

maandag, dinsdag, woensdag, donderdag, vrijdag, zaterdag, zondag — written with a **small letter**. “On Monday” = **op maandag** or just *maandag*: *Maandag werk ik.* “Every Monday” = *elke maandag* or *'s maandags*.

de ochtend (= de morgen), de middag, de avond, de nacht. As adverbs they get **'s … -s** (an old genitive, read [s]): **'s ochtends**, **'s middags**, **'s avonds**, **'s nachts**. With a day: *maandag**ochtend***, *vrijdag**avond***. Today: *vanochtend, vanmiddag, vanavond, vannacht*.
**morgen** = tomorrow; **de morgen** = the morning; **morgenochtend** = tomorrow morning. *Goedemorgen!* is a greeting until noon.
In the morning I drink coffee.
On Friday evening I'm going to the cinema.
works Saturday morning, free in the afternoon
Say which days you work or study and when you are free.

Many Dutch verbs have a stressed prefix that **splits off** and goes to the **end** of the sentence: **op**staan → *Ik **sta** om zeven uur **op**.* **thuis**komen → *Ik **kom** om zes uur **thuis**.* **op**bellen → *Ik **bel** je morgen **op**.*
With a modal verb they stay together
When the verb is an infinitive at the end (after willen, moeten, kunnen, gaan), it is written as **one word**: *Ik moet morgen vroeg **opstaan**.* *Wil je **meekomen**?*
Verbs with unstressed **be-, ge-, ver-, ont-, her-** never split: **ont**bijten → *Ik ontbijt om acht uur.* **be**ginnen → *De film begint om acht uur.* **ver**trekken → *De trein vertrekt nu.*
eten: ik eet, jij eet, hij eet, wij eten. lezen: ik lees, hij leest. slapen: ik slaap, hij slaapt.
“The film starts at eight.” (beginnen is NOT separable)
I want to get up early tomorrow.
I go to bed at eleven.
What time does Anna get up?
How does she get to work?
What does she do after work?
does the shopping and goes home
gets up at 6:30, goes to bed at 11
Describe your morning: when you get up, what you eat, when you leave.

In a Dutch main clause the **conjugated verb is in position 2**. If something other than the subject comes first (a time, a place), the **subject moves behind the verb**: *Ik kijk **'s avonds** tv.* → ***'s Avonds** kijk **ik** tv.* *Ik ga **daarna** naar huis.* → ***Daarna** ga **ik** naar huis.*
When **je/jij** comes after the verb, the **-t** is dropped: *Je werk**t** morgen.* → *Morgen werk je.* *Je kom**t** mee.* → *Kom je mee?*

altijd (always) → meestal (usually) → vaak (often) → soms (sometimes) → nooit (never). They stand right after the verb (and subject): *Ik eet **altijd** thuis.* *'s Ochtends drink ik **meestal** koffie.*
van … tot … = from … until …: Ik werk van negen tot vijf.
Start with ’s avonds: “I watch TV in the evening.”
“Are you working tomorrow?” (je after the verb)
At eight I go to work.
After that I do the shopping.
On Saturday I have to work.
In the evening I read a book.
What does Anna do first in the morning?
What does she do in the evening?
cooks, then watches TV or reads
usually by train, sometimes by bus
Describe your day in 4–5 sentences. Start at least three sentences with a time word (Om … uur, Eerst, Dan, Daarna, ’s Avonds).
start a sentence with a time word

**Heb je zaterdag tijd?** — Are you free on Saturday? **Kom je mee?** — Are you coming along? **Zullen we naar de bioscoop gaan?** — Shall we go to the cinema? **Heb je zin om uit te gaan?** — Do you feel like going out?

Yes: **Ja, gezellig!** / **Ja, leuk!** / **Prima.** No: **Helaas, ik kan niet.** (Unfortunately I can't.) / **Zaterdag kan ik niet, maar zondag wel.** (Not Saturday, but Sunday I can.) Maybe: **Misschien.**

**Hoe laat spreken we af?** — What time shall we meet? **Waar spreken we af?** — Where shall we meet? **Om half acht voor de bioscoop.** **Tot zaterdag! / Tot dan!** — See you Saturday! / See you then!
gezellig is a very Dutch word: cosy, pleasant, fun together. A café, an evening or a person can be gezellig.
Are you free on Friday evening?
We're meeting at half past seven.
Unfortunately, I have to work tomorrow.
Shall we go to the cinema?
When is Lisa free on Saturday?
What time does the film start?
Where and when do they meet?
at 7:30 in front of the cinema
Are you free on Saturday? I'm going to the cinema. Are you coming?
Invite a friend out: ask if they're free, say what you'll do, and suggest a time and place.
On the way: town, directions, transport

Tourist: Excuse me, madam, may I ask you something? I'm looking for the station.
Woman: The station? That's not far. Go straight on here as far as the traffic lights.
Tourist: Straight on to the traffic lights.
Woman: Yes. Turn left there. Then take the second street on the right.
Tourist: The second street on the right.

Buildings are a mix, so learn each one with its article. **het**: station, museum, ziekenhuis, postkantoor, restaurant, café, hotel, park, plein, stadhuis, centrum. **de**: bank, kerk, apotheek, winkel, school, straat, brug, gracht, halte, stad.

**Waar is het station?** — Where is the station? **Is er hier een bank?** — Is there a bank here? **Is er een apotheek in de buurt?** — Is there a pharmacy nearby? Answer: *Ja, in de Kerkstraat.* / *Nee, hier niet.*
A gracht is a canal inside a town with houses along it — Amsterdam is famous for them.
Where do you go when you are ill?
Where do you wait for the bus?
The museum is in the centre.
Is there a post office here?
The bank is in the Kerkstraat.
the town hall and the church are on the square

Name four places in your town and say where one of them is.
**in** de straat, **in** het centrum, **in** de stad · **op** het plein, **op** de hoek, **op** het station · **aan** de gracht, **aan** het water. These don't follow one rule — learn them as pairs.
**Is het ver?** — Is it far? *Nee, het is dichtbij.* / *Ja, ongeveer twee kilometer.* / *Het is vijf minuten lopen.* (It's a five-minute walk.)
The stop is in front of the hospital.

The park is behind the station.

between the pharmacy and the hotel

For an instruction use the **verb stem** (the ik-form), with no subject: **Ga** rechtdoor. **Neem** de eerste straat links. **Loop** tot het stoplicht. **Steek** de straat **over** (separable!). Polite, to a stranger: stem + **-t u**: **Gaat u** rechtdoor. **Neemt u** de tweede straat rechts.

**rechtdoor** straight on · **linksaf / rechtsaf** (turn) left / right · **de eerste / tweede / derde straat links** the first / second / third street on the left · **tot** het stoplicht — as far as the lights · **bij** het kruispunt — at the crossroads.

**Pardon, mag ik u iets vragen?** — Excuse me, may I ask you something? **Ik zoek het station.** — I'm looking for the station. **Weet u waar de bank is?** — Do you know where the bank is? **Hoe kom ik bij het museum?** — How do I get to the museum?
weten: ik weet, jij weet, hij weet, wij weten. “Dat weet ik niet.” = I don't know.
“Take the second street on the left.”
“Do you know where the bank is?”
At the crossroads you turn left.
Go straight on and take the first street on the left.
Excuse me, sir, I'm looking for the pharmacy.
At the traffic lights you turn right.
How do I get to the station?
What is the tourist looking for?
What should he do at the traffic lights?
opposite the park, after the bridge
straight to the crossroads, then right; the bank is on the corner
the bank is behind the station
Excuse me, madam, do you know where the station is?

By a vehicle = **met de**: *met de trein, met de bus, met de fiets, met de auto* (but *met het vliegtuig*). On foot = **lopend** or *te voet*. To a place = **naar**: *Ik ga met de trein naar Utrecht.* Order: **time – manner – place**: *Ik ga morgen met de fiets naar mijn werk.*

**in**stappen (get on) · **uit**stappen (get off) · **over**stappen (change): *Ik **stap** in Utrecht **over**.* *Waar moet ik **uitstappen**?* In the Netherlands you travel with an **ov-chipkaart**: you **check in** when you get on and **check uit** when you get off.

**Hoe lang duurt de reis?** — How long does the journey take? *De reis duurt een uur.* **rijden** — to drive / to run (of a bus or train): *De bus rijdt elk kwartier.* (The bus runs every quarter of an hour.)
The Netherlands has more bicycles than people. “Ik ga met de fiets” or simply “Ik fiets naar mijn werk.”
Where do I get off? — At the station.
We're going to Rotterdam by car.
You have to change in Leiden.
The bus stops in front of the hospital.
Where do I have to get off?
usually by bike, by tram when it rains
an hour by train with one change

At the station: buying a ticket

**Een enkeltje Utrecht, alstublieft.** — A single to Utrecht, please. **Een retour Den Haag.** — A return to The Hague. **Eerste of tweede klas?** — First or second class? No preposition is needed before the city.

**Hoe laat vertrekt de trein naar …?** — What time does the train to … leave? **Van welk spoor?** — From which platform? **Moet ik overstappen?** — Do I have to change? **Hoe laat komt de trein aan?** — What time does the train arrive? **Heeft de trein vertraging?** — Is the train delayed?
Dutch loves diminutives in **-je** (**-tje, -pje, -etje**), and they are always **het**-words: het kaart**je** (ticket), het enkel**tje**, het huis**je**, het kop**je** koffie.
Announcements say: “De trein naar Utrecht van 10.15 uur vertrekt van spoor 5.”

Does the traveller have to change?

the train leaves ten minutes early
the train leaves from platform ten

Assistant: Good afternoon. Can I help you?
Customer: Yes, please. I'm looking for a warm coat for the winter.
Assistant: What size are you?
Customer: Size 40, I think.
Assistant: And which colour would you like?
Customer: Black or dark blue.
Assistant: This black coat is very nice. And that blue one over there is in the sale.
Customer: May I try them both on?
Assistant: Of course. The fitting room is there, next to the till.
(a little later)
Customer: The black one is too small. The blue one fits well, but it's a bit long.
Assistant: It really suits you! And it's cheaper than the black one: eighty euros.
Customer: All right, I'll take the blue one.

On Saturday I have a party. What shall I wear? I have a red dress, but it's too cold for winter. My black trousers are nice, but a bit old. My sister says: ‘Put on your new green skirt with that white blouse. That suits you.’ I like the green skirt better than the black trousers too. And which shoes? The brown boots are the warmest, but the black shoes are the nicest. I'll take the black shoes. It's a party!

**dragen** — to wear (in general): *Ik draag vaak een spijkerbroek.* **aanhebben** — to have on right now: *Wat heb je aan? — Ik heb een trui aan.* **aantrekken** — to put on: *Ik trek mijn jas aan.* **uittrekken** — to take off: *Trek je schoenen uit.* All three with aan/uit are separable.
Singular in Dutch, plural in English

**de broek** (trousers), **de bril** (glasses), **de spijkerbroek** (jeans) are singular: *De broek **is** lang.* Plurals: schoen → schoen**en**, laars → laar**zen**, sok → sok**ken**, jas → jas**sen**, trui → trui**en**, jurk → jurk**en**, rok → rok**ken**.
dragen: ik draag, jij draagt, hij draagt, wij dragen. “de kleren” is always plural; “de kleding” is singular.
What do you wear on your feet?
What do you wear on your hands in winter?
I often wear jeans and a T-shirt.
In summer I wear a dress.
put on your coat and take your scarf
Say what you're wearing today and what you wear in winter.

Before a noun, an adjective almost always gets **-e**: *de rod**e** jurk, het rod**e** T-shirt, een rod**e** jurk, rod**e** schoenen*. **One exception**: **een + het-word** (singular, indefinite) — **no -e**: *een roo**d** T-shirt, een nieu**w** huis, een klei**n** kind.* After the noun there is never an ending: *De jurk is roo**d**.*

The usual spelling rules apply: a long vowel loses a letter — r**oo**d → r**o**de, gr**oo**t → gr**o**te, g**ee**l → g**e**le; a short vowel doubles the consonant — wi**t** → wi**tt**e, di**k** → di**kk**e, du**n** → du**nn**e; **s → z**, **f → v**: grij**s** → grij**z**e, lie**f** → lie**v**e.
rood, blauw, geel, groen, zwart, wit, grijs, bruin, oranje, roze, paars. **licht**blauw = light blue, **donker**groen = dark green. *oranje* and *roze* never change.
I'm looking for a blue jumper.
a long black skirt and a white blouse
Describe three pieces of clothing you own, with colours.
This and that: deze, die, dit, dat
These trousers are too small, but those trousers over there are fine.
This T-shirt is nice. — Which T-shirt? — That red one.
You can drop the noun; the adjective keeps **-e**: *Ik neem **de blauwe**.* (I'll take the blue one.) *Welke wil je? — **Die zwarte**.* There is no word for “one”.

**Ik vind** die jas mooi. — I think that coat is nice. **Wat vind je van** deze schoenen? — What do you think of these shoes? **Het staat je goed.** — It suits you. **Het zit goed.** — It fits well. **te** = too: *te groot, te duur*; **een beetje** = a bit; **erg / heel** = very.
welk/welke works like dit/deze: welk overhemd? (het) — welke jas? welke schoenen? (de / plural).
“What do you think of these shoes?”
I think that green coat is nice.
The trousers fit well, but they're a bit long.
nice but too loose — take the other one
You're shopping with a friend. Give your opinion on two things (deze/die/dit/dat, te, mooi…).

Comparative = adjective + **-er**; superlative = **het** + adjective + **-st(e)**: mooi — mooi**er** — **het** mooi**st**. Spelling rules apply: gr**oo**t → gr**o**ter, d**i**k → di**kk**er. After **r** you add **-der**: duu**r** → duur**der**, ve**r** → ver**der**. Dutch never uses *meer* for this the way English uses “more”.
**-er dan** = -er than: *Deze jas is warmer **dan** die.* **even … als** = as … as: *Deze broek is **even** duur **als** die.* **niet zo … als** = not as … as.
The comparative and superlative also take **-e** before a noun: *een goedkop**ere** jas, de mooi**ste** jurk, het groot**ste** huis.*
graag – liever – het liefst: Ik drink graag thee. Ik drink liever koffie. Ik drink het liefst water.
“This coat is warmer than that one.”
The brown boots are the warmest.
That coat is more expensive than this one.
The blue one is cheaper than the black one.
Why doesn't she wear the red dress?
the new green skirt with the white blouse
Which shoes does she choose, and why?
the black shoes — they're the nicest
the brown boots — they're the warmest
the black is nicer; the grey is cheaper and warmer
Compare two things you own (clothes, phones, bags) with -er dan.
**Kan ik u helpen?** — Can I help you? **Welke maat hebt u?** — What size are you? **De paskamer is daar.** — The fitting room is there. **Het staat u goed.** — It suits you.

**Ik kijk alleen even.** — I'm just looking. **Ik zoek een …** — I'm looking for a … **Mag ik deze passen?** — May I try this on? **Hebt u deze in maat 40?** — Do you have this in size 40? **Hebt u iets anders / een andere kleur?** — Do you have something else / another colour? **Ik neem hem / het / ze.** — I'll take it / them.

Things are **hij** (de-words) or **het** (het-words): *De jas? **Hij** is te klein.* *Het overhemd? **Het** is mooi.* As an object: **hem / het / ze**: *Ik neem **hem**.* (the coat) *Ik neem **ze**.* (the shoes)
In the sale: “50% korting” = 50% off. Keep “het bonnetje” if you want to “ruilen” (exchange).
Can I help you? — No, thank you, I'm just looking.
Do you have this coat in another colour?
May I try these shoes on?
What is the customer looking for?
What is wrong with the black coat?
Which coat does the customer buy?
the blue one, for eighty euros
the shoes are reduced from 100 to 60 euros
Good afternoon, I'm looking for black trousers in size 38.

What did you do? The past: weekend and holidays

Sanne: Hi Mark! How was your weekend?
Mark: Really nice. On Saturday I slept in and then did the shopping. In the evening I went out with friends. We ate in town and then went dancing.
Sanne: Lovely! And Sunday?
Mark: On Sunday I stayed at home. I cleaned the house and read a book. And you? What did you do?
Sanne: I went to my parents in Groningen. It was my mother's birthday. We had cake and I gave her a nice present.
Mark: Nice! Did you go by train?
Sanne: Yes, but the train was an hour late. I didn't get home until eleven.

Dear Grandma,
We've been in France for a week now. The journey was long: we sat in the car for twelve hours! But the campsite is wonderful, close to the sea. The weather is lovely. Yesterday we went to the beach and swam all day. Dad lay in the sun too long and went completely red. Today we visited an old little town. I took a lot of photos and bought a small present for you. Have you already got our card from Paris?
See you next week!
Lots of love, Emma
The perfect tense: ik heb gewerkt
How to talk about the past

In everyday speech the past is the **perfect**: a form of **hebben** in position 2 and the **past participle at the end**: *Ik **heb** gisteren **gewerkt**.* *Wij **hebben** soep **gekookt**.* Question: ***Heb** je gisteren **gewerkt**?*

Take the stem and add **ge-** in front and **-t** or **-d** at the end. Use **-t** if the stem ends in one of the consonants of **'t kofschip** (t, k, f, s, ch, p); otherwise **-d**: wer**k**en → ge·werk·**t**, ma**k**en → gemaak**t**, fie**ts**en → gefiets**t**; wo**n**en → gewoon**d**, le**r**en → geleer**d**, spe**l**en → gespeel**d**.

Look at the **infinitive** stem: rei**z**en → stem *reis*, but the z counts → gerei**sd**; le**v**en → gelee**fd**. A stem already ending in t or d gets no extra letter: wachten → gewach**t**, praten → gepraa**t**.
Time words for the past: gisteren, gisteravond, vanochtend, vorige week, vorig jaar, een jaar geleden (a year ago).
Did you watch TV last night?
talked to my sister this morning
will talk to my sister tomorrow
Say three things you did yesterday with regular verbs.
Many common verbs are **strong**: the participle ends in **-en** and the vowel often changes. They have to be learned by heart.
No ge- with be-, ver-, ont-, ge-, her-

Verbs that start with an unstressed prefix get **no ge-**: **be**ginnen → begonnen, **ver**geten → vergeten, **be**talen → betaald, **ver**tellen → verteld, **be**zoeken → bezocht, **ont**moeten → ontmoet, **ge**bruiken → gebruikt.

*Heb je **al** gegeten?* — Have you eaten yet? *Nee, **nog niet**.* — Not yet. *Heb je **ooit** haring gegeten?* — Have you ever eaten herring? *Ik heb **net** koffie gedronken.* — I've just had coffee.
I've just had a cup of coffee.
Have you read the paper yet?
yes, has just eaten a roll
Ask a friend three questions about yesterday (eten, zien, doen…).
zijn or hebben? Ik ben gegaan

Verbs of **movement to a place** or **change of state** form the perfect with **zijn**: *Ik **ben** naar huis **gegaan**.* *Hij **is** laat **gekomen**.* Also **zijn** and **blijven** themselves: *Ik **ben** ziek **geweest**.* *Wij **zijn** thuis **gebleven**.*

Verbs like **lopen, fietsen, rijden, vliegen, zwemmen** take **zijn** when a **destination** is given, and **hebben** when it's just the activity: *Ik **ben** naar het station gelopen.* — *Ik **heb** een uur gelopen.*

For **zijn** and **hebben** the simple past is more common than the perfect: **ik was, wij waren** (I was, we were); **ik had, wij hadden** (I had, we had). *Het **was** leuk.* *We **hadden** geen tijd.* *Hoe **was** je weekend?*
On Sunday we stayed at home.
The weather was nice and we had a lot of time.
cycled to the beach and swam there
Say where you went last weekend and how it was.
Separable verbs in the perfect · my weekend

With a separable verb, **ge** goes **between** the prefix and the verb, written as one word: op·staan → **opgestaan**, uit·gaan → **uitgegaan**, op·bellen → **opgebeld**, schoon·maken → **schoongemaakt**, thuis·komen → **thuisgekomen**.

Use time words first and remember inversion: ***Zaterdag** heb **ik** uitgeslapen. **Daarna** heb **ik** boodschappen gedaan. **'s Avonds** ben **ik** uitgegaan.* Add how it was: *Het was gezellig / leuk / saai / lekker.*
**Ik ben jarig.** — It's my birthday. **Gefeliciteerd (met je verjaardag)!** — Happy birthday! In the Netherlands you also congratulate the family: *Gefeliciteerd met je moeder!*
On Sunday I stayed at home.
We ate in town and then we danced.
What did Mark do on Saturday evening?
went out with friends: dinner and dancing
What did Mark do on Sunday?
Why did Sanne go to Groningen?
Why did Sanne get home late?
the train was an hour late
got up at six, so very tired now
Write 5 sentences about your last weekend. Start at least two with a time word and use both hebben and zijn.

**op vakantie gaan** — to go on holiday: *We zijn naar Frankrijk op vakantie geweest.* **in het buitenland** — abroad. **op de camping / in een hotel**. **aan zee / in de bergen**. *We zijn met de auto gegaan.*

When two actions share the same helper verb, you can say it once: *Ik **heb** veel foto's **gemaakt** en een cadeautje **gekocht**.* With inversion in the second part: *Gisteren **zijn** we naar het strand gegaan en **hebben** we gezwommen.*
A card starts with “Lieve …” (to family and friends) or “Beste …”, and ends with “Groetjes” or “Veel liefs”.
How do you start a card to a friend?
Yesterday we went to the beach.
I took a lot of photos and bought a present.
he lay in the sun too long and went red
visited an old town, took photos, bought a present
flew to Italy last year and stayed in a small seaside hotel
